en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Questions of King Divākara, spoken by the Buddha;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Great Teacher of the Dharma at Nālandā Monastery in Magadha, Central India.
The Śramaṇa Dharma Heaven, a Subject invested with the purple robe, translated by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Kuśīlavana in Kauśāmbī, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, as well as a multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the woman Anupamā Māṅgī became filled with anger and, out of malice and jealousy toward Queen Śyāmāvatī, spoke to King Divākara, saying:
"Does Your Majesty know?..."
The queen Śamavati and five hundred other women have all engaged in sexual misconduct with that śramaṇa.
I now inform you, O Son of Heaven, that this is truly unforgivable.

At that time, having heard the words of the maiden Anupamā-Māṇavikā, King Divākara was overcome with extreme rage; his mind could not endure it, and intending to kill Queen Śyāmāvatī, he seized his bow with his hand and released an arrow, shooting her.

At that time, Queen Śāntā entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). The arrow discharged by the king rose into the air and burst into flames; the blaze grew fierce and intense, yet the arrow turned back and, rushing toward King Divodāsa, came to rest on his left side. Protected by the Buddha’s secret guardianship, the arrow did not strike his body, nor did it cause him any injury or disturbance.
At that time, King Divākara was seized with terror; his hair stood on end, and he fell to the ground, only to rise once more.
He questioned Queen Śamāvatī, speaking in verse:
"Are you a goddess, a female spirit, or a rākṣasī?"
"Gaṇḍā, Pūtanā, and the others?
Thus I ask you: how do you practice?"
Never before seen, never before heard, nor even known:
there has never been a woman whom weapons could not wound.
Well-trained in the art of archery, my arrows are never released in vain.
Never has an arrow been shot in vain.
Whether against monkeys or birds, or even against human targets,
there has never been one that did not strike its mark.
Just as this arrow I have now released returns and stays before my face, Without harming or injuring my body;
I now take refuge in you, Praying that you will save me from my suffering and distress.
Listen attentively to these truthful words: I intended to kill you on purpose.
Forgive my transgression and do not give rise to anger; consider this a good deed that has caused me to be freed from suffering and distress, so that such a thing shall never happen again.
At that time, Queen Śāntā replied to King Divākara, speaking in verse:
"I am not a celestial maiden, nor am I a Gandharva maiden;
I am neither a ghost nor a Rākṣasa—I am Śāntā."
I have become a disciple of the Buddha; for the sake of that great compassion, my mind practices virtue.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons, I contemplate that wholesome compassion.
Therefore, I practice the conduct of loving-kindness.
Seeing those who perceive reality as it is, yet being destroyed like a crop that has ripened but is ruined by thunder and hail.
I and they both delight in this: that all the World-Honored Ones are far removed from sensual desire.
Furthermore, I have heard the World-Honored One say:
"The Buddha and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, the Pratyekabuddhas and the Śrāvakas—
all have completely abandoned female forms.
Universally overcome by Māra, they remain free from the defilement of attachment to women."
One can attain peace and happiness of body, and ultimately achieve liberation.
But sentient beings lacking wisdom do not distance themselves from craving and desire;
they commit boundless sinful karma and fall into the three evil realms.
The bottomless pit of desire’s fire blazes with fierce flames that never cease.
Those with wisdom delight in liberation and are not defiled by female beauty.
Upon seeing her, one is immediately bound; she speaks falsely of empty pleasure.
Falling among sentient beings, they die and enter perilous evil paths.
Do not listen to the words of women, nor be angry with me;
let your heart give rise to joy and resolve to take refuge in the World-Honored One.
"If you wish to seek an audience with the Buddha, I shall go with the Great King;
once we have arrived there, listen attentively, for he will surely preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
At that time, King Divākara addressed Queen Śyāmavatī:
"At that very moment, you must quickly go to the presence of the World-Honored One.

Surrounded by the king, ministers, and citizens in attendance, they beheld the Great Muni, majestic and dignified like a great mountain of gold, blazing with radiant light and adorned with auspicious splendor. They also saw the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, all surrounding the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Great King prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I have encountered an unprecedented matter, the likes of which I have never before heard or seen. Now that I have come to the presence of the Buddha, may the World-Honored One, out of your compassion, explain it to me."
The World-Honored One said:
“Great King! What you have spoken is an unprecedented matter.”
The king spoke again, saying:
"Today, due to matters of lust within my palace, the woman Upamānīkā conceived a malicious intent and slanderously declared:
'The lady Śamavati has engaged in sexual misconduct with a śrāvaka śramaṇa.'"

Upon hearing these words, my anger and resentment reached their utmost limit; I killed Queen Śyāmāvatī by shooting an arrow at her. From that arrow, flames emerged, blazing and fiercely radiant, yet they turned back to stay at my left side and did not harm my body.
The lady Śamāvatī prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and spoke these words: "That king asked me:
'Are you a goddess, a nāga maiden, a gandharva maiden, a piśāca maiden, a preta maiden, or a rākṣasa maiden?'"
"What practice have you cultivated that you have become thus?
He replied to the king, saying:
"I am the queen of the Great King; I am not a goddess, nor a nāga girl, nor a gandharva girl, nor a piśācī, nor a rākṣasī."
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and his disciples whose minds are virtuous and purely clean are like those devas.
At that time, Lady Śamāvatī praised the merits of the World-Honored One:

"Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, possesses such an awakening of a Worthy and Perfectly Enlightened One; he possesses such great kindness and great compassion; he is endowed with great merit and wisdom; he has achieved great majestic power and attained great sovereignty."
"For what reason?
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is the teacher of gods and humans; may he deign to witness this sincerity.
At that time, King Divākara, before the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus, confessed and revealed his transgressions:
"We were like ignorant children, with minds as deluded as if we were in darkness, and lacking roots of goodness; thus, when we thought of the Tathāgata’s śrāvakas, we gave rise to slander."
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will resolve our doubts and regrets so that we may receive and uphold [this teaching].
The World-Honored One said:
"Give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, uphold the practice of the precepts, and bring extensive benefit to sentient beings.
King Divākara then rose from his seat and joined his palms in reverent salutation.
The Buddha said,
"Great King! Simply sit at ease."
Then King Divākara prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
King Divākara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My mind was so impetuous that I listened to the words of a woman; I have committed sinful karma and suffer its consequences, knowing that at the end of my life I shall fall into hell.
How excellent, World-Honored One!
"I pray that you will speak of the faults of women.
The World-Honored One replied:

"The activities of women are manifold; they delude and confuse sentient beings, feigning extraordinary appearances, being sycophantic and deceitful, lacking sincerity in heart, and engaging in inverted thoughts, flattery, and hypocrisy. In their movements and actions, they insistently seek intimacy, binding sentient beings and constantly practicing perverse conduct; you must be mindful of this and awaken to it."
The king said:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will grant me your compassion and listen to what I have to say.”
"World-Honored One, from this day forward, I shall not draw near to women, nor shall I commit any sinful karma on account of women. Since I shall commit no sin, I shall not fall into hell."
"Just as I have long sought to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Furthermore, King Divākara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having heard this meaning of desire from the Buddha, I truly understand that it is because of women that one receives such evil retribution.”
The Buddha said, “Great King!
Female beauty is deep-seated and firm; it gives birth to parents who are enemies and parents who are violent and evil. If one gives rise to attachment and delight toward it, one will fall into hell.”
"Therefore, women have such faults as these.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"If one were to calculate the faults of a man's lustful desires, your parents and kinsmen in future lives would also share in those faults.
King Divākara said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
Excellent, excellent!
You have explained the faults of a man to me; what are the faults of a man, and how do his parents and kinsmen also share in those faults?
The Buddha said:
"Great King! Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well!
I shall speak for you.
Thus the World-Honored One addressed him.
“Great King! There are four kinds of faults in a man.
The Great King asked:
“What are the four faults?
The World-Honored One replied, “Great King!”

If a man is addicted to sensual desire and becomes intoxicated by it, through that intoxication his mind becomes perverted; because of this perversion, he develops deep attachment and delight for women, and consequently has no desire to see or hear of those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas within the community of bhikṣus who possess moral discipline and virtuous conduct.

Because they do not wish to see, hear, or associate with śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who maintain the precepts and possess virtuous conduct, they neither draw near to them, nor take refuge in them, nor make offerings to them; likewise, they distance themselves from those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who lack both precepts and conduct.

Furthermore, they lack the faculty of faith, do not cultivate virtuous conduct, do not practice giving, and possess no wisdom at all; being of little learning and meager merit, they are arrogant and conceited, engaging in the behavior of ghosts and spirits.

Furthermore, they associate with the ignorant, are greedily attached to evil dharmas, and take delight in foul impurities; they distance themselves from virtuous friends, and even if they are born among gods or humans, they constantly revile and disparage their own lives.

They do not perform *homa* offerings for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; they distance themselves from the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; and they turn their backs upon the fruit and virtue of *nirvāṇa*. For a long time, they dwell in recollection of women, courtesans, song, dance, drinking, and laughter. Bound by such fetters, when they eventually die, they fall into the Saṃghāta, Kālasūtra, Saṃjīva, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci hells, where they undergo various sufferings.
From the hells they are born into the realm of Yama;
among the animal realm they are born as lions, tigers, wolves, and various evil birds and beasts;
even down to the bodies of *piśācas*, who dwell upon the iron-fork trees.
"Great King!
If a man acts in such a foolish manner and receives this evil retribution, this is the first fault of a man.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Sensual desire is foul and impure at its root; once it has passed, the suffering of karma constantly increases.
The wise Dharma-master reviles such defilement, for even one's own parents would find no benefit in it."
Just as a vast pit of impurity, filled with excrement and soil, reeking with foul stench,
or like a bloated corpse amidst a cemetery— so too is one who indulges in lustful desire.

Furthermore, it is like flies and insects gnawing at a festering sore, or like donkeys and horses rushing to sleep amidst filth and excrement, or like pigs and dogs devouring putrid fish; such is the nature of indulging in and craving women.

They destroy their good reputation as well as their virtuous conduct; constantly practicing the violation of precepts and devoid of shame, they fail to be reborn in the heavenly realms and instead fall into the Avīci hell. For this reason, the Dharma Master censures sensual desire.
Just as one who has mistakenly drunk a potent poison Becomes delirious, frantic, and suffers pain throughout the body,
Failing to realize they have been struck by the poison of impermanence— So too is it with those who indulge in sensual desires.
Delighting in fine flavors and exquisite delicacies, Craving the sound of song and clinging to sights and sounds, One neglects household duties and forgets much;
Doing nothing but accumulating the causes of suffering within saṃsāra.

Clinging with greed to sensual desires, they constantly praise them; failing to understand that this deluded body is but a bag of excrement, they perpetually engage in base conduct day and night, and with meager merit, sink into the miserable realms.
Praising lustful conduct as non-conduct, abounding in anger and increasing ignorance—
like treading upon a steep and perilous precipice, one does not realize that in an instant life may be lost.
Having already parted from the human world of Jambudvīpa, one falls into the boundless ocean of karma;
surrounded by five peaks amidst iron mountains, the light of the sun, moon, and lamps is entirely unseen.
Like a mad wind, chaotic and devoid of understanding, wandering back and forth, traversing every direction while losing its way;
thus one passes through births, dwelling eternally here, held in no esteem by any in the world,
and incapable of generating any kind of wholesome karma.
They abandon and turn their backs on their honored parents to commit the five heinous crimes; yet they are doubly diligent in consorting with their wives and daughters.
They cast wide the net of sin without reflection, falling into the midst of greed, delusion, and sensual pleasure.
Parents depart without returning; they think not of their upbringing or the hardships endured for them.
Indulging in negligence, lust, and frivolity, their mutual afflictions increase manifold.
Destroying practice and harboring various doubts, one fails to meet the worthy and holy as a cause for excellence;
delighting in perverse conduct, one undergoes extreme suffering, disregarding both punishment and the invasion of shame.
Quarreling, deceiving, and plundering lead to injury and death; They squander wealth and alienate virtuous friends.
Such acts prevent rebirth in the heavenly realms or the human world, And cause one to enter the Avīci Hell after death.
The Iron Forest is azure with dense, jagged blades; fierce flames and glowing embers fill the City of Fire.
Sword-trees and knife-mountains cover the ground, while molten copper and hot iron serve as broth and food.
Such great suffering arises from lustful desire, which obscures the roots of bodhi-wisdom.
You should inspire fear in women and not allow them to come near and give rise to attachment;
if you remain aligned with the wholesome paths of humans and devas, before long you will attain enlightenment yourself.
"Furthermore, Great King!
When parents give birth to a son, the matter is exceedingly difficult, as is well known to the world.

While dwelling in the womb, they carry the burden for ten months, undergoing manifold kinds of suffering and pain; rising and sitting are arduous, and their intake of food and drink must be regulated. Even when the birth is finally achieved, it is like the slaughtering of a pig or a sheep."
Disregarding her own person, she worried only for her son; nursing and raising him, how could he ever be parted from her embrace?
When he had defecated or urinated, she herself had to wash him clean.

Later, as he gradually grew up, [the father] instructed and exhorted him with various words of sincerity, causing him to study the crafts, arts, calligraphy, correspondence, arithmetic, commerce, trade, and all manner of professional activities within Jambudvīpa.

Furthermore, he provided for their physical and mental well-being, bestowed upon them vast wealth and property to enjoy, and carefully selected kinsmen to marry off wives and concubines, hoping they would be filial and obedient toward their parents, serving and supporting them with reverence; yet their minds remained deranged and utterly deluded, deeply attached to sensual desires without any realization.
Furthermore, they privately take wives and concubines from other clans; driven by mutual lust and attachment, they become unfilial and disrespectful toward their own parents.

When their fathers later grow old and decrepit—their bodies emaciated, their eyes and ears deaf and dim, and their rising and sitting made difficult requiring the support of others—they instead harbor hatred, slight, abandon, and loathe them. Subjecting them to various forms of oppression, they drive their fathers out of the house and gather with their wives and children from outside clans, indulging in all manner of pleasures.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"If a man commits such an evil deed as to abandon and turn his back on his parents, he will certainly enter the Avīci Hell at the end of his life, with no prospect of escape;
this constitutes the second transgression."
If, noble son, you turn your back on female form, keep your mind pure, support your parents, and practice filial piety,

then after the end of your life you shall not fall into the evil realms but will be reborn among the devas, where you will enjoy blissful fortune. When your heavenly merit is exhausted and you descend to be born in the human world, you shall not suffer from poverty or low status, but will instead possess wealth, honor, and auspiciousness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Free from desire and practicing loving-kindness and filial piety, At the end of life, one is reborn in the celestial realms;
With the body of a Brahmā King or Śakra, One constantly experiences happiness."
By honoring one's aged parents, one will later be born among humans;
entering the sea as a merchant, one will obtain precious treasures in peace and security.
By honoring one's aged parents, one possesses the most supreme virtue of all.
When the seeds sown in the field ripen into fruit, the measure of one’s merit is inexhaustible.
By providing for one's aged parents, one shall never again bear heavy burdens;
though always carried by donkeys and horses, one cannot be harmed by the edge of a blade.
By honoring one's aged parents, one shall not cross the river of salt water,
nor can fierce fires or weapons draw near.
By honoring one's aged parents, one will always obtain virtuous wives and sons.
With grain, wheat, and wealth, with lapis lazuli and precious gold,
by making offerings to one’s aged parents, one shall always dwell in celestial palaces,
surrounded on all four sides by countless gardens of joy.
Providing for one's aged parents, constantly hearing the sound of the Buddha-dharma,
possessing the marks of excellence and a dignified appearance—
who would not revere such a person? Furthermore, Great King!

If that man performs unrighteous deeds, his mind is not sincere, he is constantly full of wrong views, lacks knowledge of the wholesome, and gives rise to delusions; he is frequently praised by those who are foolish and ignorant, while those with wisdom are always filled with indignation toward him. His sinful karma deepens further, and he forever loses great benefit; he shall never encounter the world of a Buddha, remaining arrogant and conceited, impoverished and lowly, and unloved by the multitude.
This is the third fault of such a man.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When a man engages in lustful desire, He perversely discriminates a self;
Deluded by ignorance, his karmic offenses are deep, And he wanders in saṃsāra, falling into the evil realms."
Far removed from the virtues of the Buddha, lacking the wisdom of discernment,
they vainly seek peace and happiness, like searching for a *luka* fruit in a river.
These people of delusion and lustful desire are sycophantic, crooked, and full of falsehood.
Seeking unrighteous pleasures, one instead incurs the suffering of hell.
Attached to desire, their views are inverted; base and ignorant of themselves, they are like those in the darkness of night, unable to distinguish the path from that which is not the path.
Lacking shame, remorse, and the faculty of faith, they indulge only in sounds, forms, and flavors;
neither Bodhisattvas nor Śrāvakas have ever performed offerings for them.
Even if they should encounter one who practices correctly and proclaims the subtle and wondrous sound, [they remain heedless].
Disregarding the Dharma and refusing to listen, one sinks into the hells, never again to regain a human body.
Severing the practice of generosity and other virtues, one remains lost and fails to cultivate; thus, the supreme state of Bodhi is forfeited.
"Furthermore, Great King!

If men, for the sake of their own livelihood and out of attachment to sensual desire, being obstructed by ignorance and folly, engage in various crafts and diverse occupations—such as writing, accounting, chanting, and debate; or associate with kings and ministers, practice unrighteous conduct, inflict punishments upon sentient beings, employ all manner of deceptions to extensively seek wealth and profit, and commit various evil deeds."

Furthermore, for the sake of their own livelihood, they engage in unwholesome conduct, trading in oxen, donkeys, camels, horses, pigs, sheep, chickens, and dogs, even performing such tasks as incantations against dragons, setting snares for rabbits, or acting as executioners.

Or again, they may engage in commerce, choosing no safe path, but wandering instead upon treacherous and evil roads, foul and filthy paths, and ways where bands of thieves with swords and blades prowl; even crossing the vast, deep ocean, enduring cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and all manner of suffering in their pursuit of wealth and profit.
Furthermore, regarding śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, he was stingy and greedy, refusing to practice giving and remaining single-mindedly attached to sensual desires.

Moreover, he was subdued and driven by women like a slave; having lived together with them for a long time, he never parted from them. Whether rising or sitting, in conversation or mutual glances, they were deeply enamored with one another.
"Therefore, to keep women as concubines and have them enter hell together after their lives end constitutes the fourth fault.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
For one who pursues sensual desires, how can there ever be joy in intoxication?
Seeking after base things through delusion, how could such a person find peace and happiness?
This is not the work of a true man; he acts himself and does not realize his error.
Shameless as camels or donkeys, they cannot endure extreme filth and evil.
These people possess little wisdom and do not realize their roots of sin are deep;
they rush toward women like dogs rushing toward excrement.
Foul and loathsome, yet not to be enjoyed, it is that which the ignorant cherish and prize;
unaware of the faults of lustful desire, they are like the blind who do not see forms.
The fool is attached to lustful desire, like a dog rushing toward filth.
Sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—attachment to these is likewise so.
Foolish people who cling to desire wander through the various realms of existence;
like a monkey tied to a stake, they never escape the three realms.
The foolish person, deluded and attached to desire, is like a crow longing for putrid meat;
constantly led away by evil Māras, they fall into the miserable realms.
The fool craves flavors and becomes entangled in the attachment to what is beautiful.
How different from a worm in a latrine; how could one not know it to be impure?
The wise attain liberation; they cannot be defiled by female beauty.
Seeing her, they give rise to alarm and dread, casting her aside like a rotting corpse.
Foolish and harboring distraction, attached to desire and unable to renounce it,
one suffers like a traveler on a scorching road, exhausted and thirsty yet drinking salt water.
Seeing things thus, the fool loses his life through delusion.
For one who is firmly attached to sensual desire, the faults and calamities are likewise.
Truly, for the sake of this woman, it is like having a leprous sore on the body;
as worms arise and devour it from within, so too is the craving for lust.
If one adorns a woman, it is like painting a jar filled with excrement;
observing only the outward appearance, who would know the impurity within?
It is also like washing clothes in oil and then hanging them upon one's body.
Adorning women is likewise a defilement;
it is like clothing covering a sword or light ash covering a fire.
Adorning women brings about such ruin and harm.
Furthermore, when the fire at the end of an eon arises, the great earth blazes through and through;
grasses and trees are no longer seen to grow, and rivers and seas dry up completely.
Even the abodes of the bhūtas, as well as Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains, [are consumed].
The six heavens of desire and the first dhyāna—when these are destroyed, who can save them?
Thus, indulging in female beauty, the fire of lust blazes fiercely, incinerating sentient beings; such violation and ruin cannot be remedied.
The human body quickly becomes impure, composed of various foul and loathsome things:
fingers, nails, hair, and body hair; saliva and mucus, as well as nasal secretions;
filth, sweat, and excrement; fat, marrow, and the membranes of the brain.
Skin and flesh together with marrow, pus and blood connected by sinews and vessels;
spleen, kidneys, heart, and lungs; intestines, stomach, gallbladder, and liver;
the raw organs facing the cooked organs, red phlegm together with white phlegm.
Furthermore, eighty thousand households of minute insects dwell constantly within the body, devouring it;
yet the foolish person does not perceive this.
They give rise to craving and attachment for the body, just as flies long for pus and blood.
Perceiving foul odors as fragrant, they find pleasure within suffering.
Such people, who are addicted to desire, strike one another with raised staves;
as the fires of lust compete to burn them, who among those intoxicated by delusion can awaken?
The ignorant are attached to the flavor of pleasure, like a dog in an empty room, or like the sound of a *ḍiṭṭhi*; in the end, they produce only false imaginings.
Furthermore, they are like monkeys that constantly cling to trees.
Even unto reaching impermanence, one does not leave the tree;
so too the person of greedy desire, pursuing the realm of forms,
falls into the evil destinies and does not escape the suffering of birth and death.
The foolish person of lustful desire, after their life ends there,
is cast into an iron cauldron and remains there for an eon.
Floating and sinking like beans being boiled, the dimensions of that cauldron are vast.
Sixty-four koṭis of beings depend upon them;
each one who falls there cannot be measured,
as they are boiled in cauldrons, suffering for a full hundred kalpas.
For two, three, or four kalpas, according to the lightness or heaviness of their karma,
their skin and flesh both rot and decay until the bones appear like white conch shells.
Furthermore, by the power of their own karma, they grasp sharp hooks with their hands.
They are cast into glowing iron troughs; though dead, they are restored to life.
Again, they are seized by the hell-wardens, who wield iron pestles to pound them until their marrow is ground to powder;
yet, blown by the wind, they are revived once more.
Some are struck with iron clubs, split asunder as if by axes;
three, four, or five iron beasts follow behind to bite and gnaw them.
Furthermore, they are attacked by iron crows, iron dogs, and jackals.
Their fangs and beaks are as sharp as swords, devouring the brains and marrow of sinful beings.
If one commits evil karma, one will fall into the River of Excrement or onto blades and swords; everything there is foul and putrid.
If one commits sinful karma, one falls into the Extremely Hot Hell,
the Howling, the Great Howling, the Black Rope, and the Burning.
If one commits sinful karma, one falls into the River of Ashes.
Entering layer upon layer as the suffering increases, the pain becomes unbearable.
If one commits sinful karma, at death one falls into hell;
hungry, one swallows glowing iron balls, and thirsty, one drinks molten copper.
If one commits sinful karma, one falls between iron mountains;
when all the mountains close together at once, they crush the body into powder.
If one commits sinful karma, one will constantly undergo suffering and affliction.
Having obtained such a fruit as this, there is no one who can save you.
This place is not one of peace or joy; it is summoned by the karma of previous lives.
How could parents, wife, or children possibly rescue you?
The base practice of lust leads directly to the Avīci Hell, where one undergoes unbearable suffering;
this has been taught by the Buddhas of the three times.
Therefore, a base person who dwells together with women—
Like one carrying a sack of excrement, the fool wanders everywhere.
Bound by women as if by shackles and fetters,
with the fires of hell burning his body, he can find no peace or happiness.
"In an instant, wisdom arises; having thus heard the Buddha-dharma, one leaves behind all lustful desires and, having gone forth, attains liberation.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"If a man engages in sexual misconduct, he shall fall into hell and undergo such great suffering.
Therefore, Great King, constantly recollect the Buddha and the Dharma; observe your body and mind so that no transgression arises."
King Divākara said, “So be it,
World-Honored One! Having conceived deep faith toward the Tathāgata, he addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is most rare: that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has so excellently expounded the faults of women and men.

I shall receive and uphold [this teaching], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; from this day forward, I shall abandon the faults of sexual desire, weapons, and the like, and out of compassion, I shall benefit all sentient beings.”

When these words were spoken, King Divākara in the assembly, along with the bhikṣus, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, having heard what the Buddha had said, all rejoiced greatly, paid their respects, and departed.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, *The Questions of King Divaukasa* (Rājādanda-paripṛcchā-sūtra)
